items.title: 52150_Charlie Barnet oral history interview
items.q: Woody Herman stole Ralph from me... he wound up with Frances... she also sang with Woody... I think she made more records with me than she did with Woody... We had... Woody Herman [as a managed artist]

ctx.x: And how about Frances and Neal, when did they work for you? Frances Wayne and Neal Hefti?

Well, Frances worked for me in '43. She was in that band. But she was there -- she wasn't there at the Park Central. Virginia Maxie was there. Frances joined the band -- she was there when Ralph Burns was with the band. Oh, wait a minute. Ralph Burns was there. It wasn't Dodo, Dodo came a little later. Ralph was still in the band there. Because I had heard her with her brother's band, and Ralph had been playing in that, and I wound up with both of them. And then Woody Herman stole Ralph from me, and then he wound…

with Frances. I used to break bands up. I mean it got -- it was -- of course at that time, I mean, I had a reason. I told you about the draft board, you know. It was a very uneasy thing. But I think I got my kicks out of building bands.

items.title: 52220_Woody Herman oral history interview
items.q: Charlie took the other thing, -- Barnet -- and did an actual copy of Duke's music, and that to me would have been very distasteful

ctx.x: Kind of a bridge between the Duke-ish, Louis-ish period.

That's right. My earliest influences came back and Ralph was very heavily influenced by Sweetpea and by Duke and so we were all shooting for the same thing. We didn't want to be like Duke, but we sure wanted to sound good like him.

In other words, Charlie took the other thing, -- Barnet -- and did an actual copy of Duke's music, and that to me would have been very distasteful, and that would be dishonoring a great man and a great group of musicians. But what we did was try to capture the feeling, warmth and enthu-
